title: CONGENITAL MYOPATHY 10B, MILD VARIANT
alt_titles: MYOPATHY, AREFLEXIA, RESPIRATORY DISTRESS, AND DYSPHAGIA, EARLY-ONSET, MILD VARIANT

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that congenital myopathy-10B, mild variant (CMYO10B), is caused by compound heterozygous or homozygous mutation in the MEGF10 gene (612453) on chromosome 5q23.2.

checks.claim: Congenital myopathy-10B, mild variant (CMYO10B), is caused by compound heterozygous or homozygous mutation in the MEGF10 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: patients displaying a less severe phenotype, with later respiratory failure and minicores on muscle biopsy (mvEMARDD or with minicore myopathy), harbour homozygous or compound heterozygous missense variants affecting the cysteine in the EGF-like domain
checks.explanation: The paper says the mild variant (mvEMARDD) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous MEGF10 variants.

checks.evidence_quote: MEGF10 lies within a linkage peak on chromosome 5 that reached the maximum possible LOD score of 1.329.
checks.explanation: Paper places MEGF10 on chromosome 5; band is standard nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Takayama et al. (2016) stated that MEGF10 mutations cause early-onset myopathy with areflexia, respiratory distress, and dysphagia (EMARDD) as well as a milder phenotype of minicore myopathy. Congenital myopathy-10B is the milder form. It is an autosomal recessive myopathy with onset in infancy, childhood, or as late as the fifth decade. Features include axial, neck, and proximal muscle weakness, facial weakness, scoliosis, joint contractures, hypernasal speech, dysphagia, and respiratory insufficiency. Muscle biopsies show myopathic or dystrophic changes and often minicores (Boyden et al., 2012; Harris et al., 2018; Croci et al., 2022).

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) reported a nonconsanguineous Caucasian family of mixed European ancestry (family 1030) in which 3 of 4 sibs had an undiagnosed autosomal recessive myopathy that resembled multiminicore disease in some respects. Onset was in infancy, with weakness and contractures beginning in the neck. The patients had axial and proximal muscle weakness, facial weakness, and contractures of the elbows, knees, and heel cords, and some had neck muscle atrophy. Serum creatine kinase was mildly elevated. All 3 had childhood-onset scoliosis treated with spinal fusion surgery. Beginning at age 10 to 11 years, all 3 developed respiratory problems that were treated with bilevel positive airway pressure ventilation at night. All 3 had hypernasal speech. One had a cleft palate and another had a midline palatal ridge. Muscle biopsies showed fatty replacement of muscle tissue, increased endomysial and perimysial connective tissue, regenerating and moth-eaten fibers, variation in fiber size, increased internalized nuclei, type I fiber predominance, and minicores. There were no rimmed vacuoles, central cores, nemaline rods, or ragged red fibers. Boyden et al. (2012) noted palatal abnormalities in their patients and suggested that MEGF10 may influence palate formation or determination of the facial midline. However, they noted that these features are nonspecific in patients with myopathic facies.

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) also described a Caucasian girl of distant Portuguese ancestry (subject 105-1) who had been diagnosed with multiminicore disease. No other family member was affected. She presented at several weeks of age with hypotonia, which first appeared as a weak neck and floppy head. She had a markedly high-arched palate, poor feeding with failure to thrive, blue-tinged sclerae, hyperflexible joints, and frequent pulmonary infections in childhood, but she did not have chronic breathing problems. She had mild nonprogressive proximal weakness, facial weakness, deficits in motor performance, and mild scoliosis that progressed to 20 degrees. Serum CK was mildly elevated (302 U/L). Muscle biopsy showed marked variation in fiber size, internalized nuclei, and slightly increased endomysial connective tissue. Electron microscopy confirmed minicores and showed Z-band disarray. Only a single heterozygous MEGF10 variant was found in this patient (see MOLECULAR GENETICS).

paragraphs.text: Croci et al. (2022) reported a 22-year-old Italian man born to healthy consanguineous parents. There was no family history of neuromuscular disease. He was born preterm at 33 weeks with birth asphyxia, and he had a weak suck. He had no motor developmental delay or intellectual disability. However, he developed slowly progressive muscle weakness with impaired walking, rhinolalia, dysphagia, and respiratory involvement. He required nocturnal noninvasive ventilation from age 16 years and had recurrent pulmonary infections due to aspiration. Examination showed axial hypotonia, generalized muscular hypotrophy, global areflexia, cleft palate, contractures of the elbows and ankles, equinovarus foot stance, hyperlordosis, and scoliosis. Facial expression was preserved and sensation was not impaired. Serum creatine kinase, brain and spine MRI, echocardiogram, and ECG were normal. Electrophysiologic studies showed reduced amplitude of muscle evoked potentials. Muscle biopsy showed variation in fiber size, internal nuclei, fibrosis, whorled fibers, cytoplasmic inclusions, and minicores. An earlier muscle biopsy had shown only nonspecific changes, and a later one showed myofibrillar changes with minicores.

paragraphs.text: The transmission pattern of CMYO10B is autosomal recessive. In the family reported by Boyden et al. (2012), 3 sibs born to unaffected nonconsanguineous parents were affected and carried compound heterozygous MEGF10 mutations that segregated with the disorder. In the patient reported by Croci et al. (2022), born to consanguineous parents, the mutation was homozygous and both healthy parents were heterozygous carriers.

paragraphs.text: In 3 affected sibs from a nonconsanguineous family (family 1030), Boyden et al. (2012) identified compound heterozygous missense mutations in the MEGF10 gene: C326R and C774R. The mutations were found by whole-genome sequencing of 1 affected member, filtered using the linkage data. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the mutations were in trans in affected individuals and segregated with the myopathy in all 6 family members. Both mutations substituted conserved cysteines in atypical EGF-like domains that were predicted to form disulfide bonds. Neither was present in dbSNP, 1000 Genomes, or the NHLBI Exome Sequencing Project, nor in 715 and 645 genotyped unaffected controls, respectively. Boyden et al. (2012) then screened the MEGF10 open reading frame in 190 additional patients with unexplained myopathies. They found only 1 patient (subject 105-1) with a single heterozygous mutation (R71W). This patient's unaffected parent was also heterozygous for R71W, so it was not a de novo dominant mutation. The authors suggested that the patient may carry a second MEGF10 mutation that they could not detect.

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) hypothesized that loss of MEGF10 function causes excessive differentiation of satellite cells. This would deplete the self-renewing population needed to regenerate damaged muscle fibers and could explain the dystrophic features in patient biopsies. They suggested that MEGF10-related myopathy and SEPN1-related multiminicore disease may share a common mechanism of satellite cell dysfunction. In support of a role in satellite cells, Holterman et al. (2007) had found that siRNA silencing of Megf10 on isolated mouse myofibers reduced the number of activated satellite cells by 30% and the number of self-renewing Pax7+/MyoD- cells by 62%. It also increased myogenin-expressing cells 3.15-fold, indicating precocious differentiation.

checks.claim: The other MEGF10 mutation in the 66-year-old man was a c.352T-C transition resulting in a cys118-to-arg (C118R) substitution.
checks.evidence_quote: a novel missense variant (c.352T>C, p.(Cys118Arg))

paragraphs.text: For discussion of the c.352T-C transition in the MEGF10 gene, resulting in a cys118-to-arg (C118R) substitution, which Harris et al. (2018) found in a 66-year-old man with adult-onset CMYO10B, see c.1426+1G-T.

checks.claim: Harris et al. (2018) found the MEGF10 c.352T-C (C118R) variant in a 66-year-old man with adult-onset CMYO10B.
checks.evidence_quote: a novel missense variant (c.352T>C, p.(Cys118Arg))
checks.explanation: Variant found in the 66-year-old man with adult-onset MEGF10 myopathy.

paragraphs.text: In a 22-year-old Italian man born to consanguineous parents who had a progressive congenital myopathy with minicores, Croci et al. (2022) identified a homozygous c.2096G-C transversion (NM_001256545.2) in the MEGF10 gene, resulting in a cys699-to-ser (C699S) substitution. The mutation was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Both healthy parents were heterozygous carriers. The variant was not present in ClinVar or gnomAD and affected a conserved cysteine in an EGF-like domain. The authors classified it as likely pathogenic by ACMG criteria.

checks.claim: Croci et al. (2022) studied a 22-year-old Italian man born to consanguineous parents.
checks.evidence_quote: This patient is a 22-year-old boy, born to healthy consanguineous parents
checks.explanation: The paper elsewhere identifies him as the first Italian patient.

checks.claim: The 22-year-old Italian man reported by Croci et al. (2022) had a progressive congenital myopathy with minicores.
checks.evidence_quote: a progressive form of mvEMARDD with myofibrillar alterations at muscle biopsy
checks.explanation: The case report notes congenital onset, and the second biopsy showed minicores.

checks.claim: Croci et al. (2022) identified a homozygous c.2096G-C transversion (NM_001256545.2) in the MEGF10 gene, resulting in a cys699-to-ser (C699S) substitution, in the 22-year-old Italian man.
checks.evidence_quote: Exome sequencing led to the identification of the homozygous variant (NM_001256545.2): c.2096G > C (p.Cys699Ser) in the MEGF10 gene.

checks.claim: The MEGF10 C699S mutation was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing.
checks.evidence_quote: The candidate pathogenic variant in MEGF10 was confirmed by Sanger sequencing and segregation was performed in the healthy parents.

checks.claim: Both healthy parents of the 22-year-old Italian man were heterozygous carriers of the MEGF10 C699S variant.
checks.evidence_quote: Sanger sequencing was also performed and confirmed that the patient was homozygous for the variant, and both parents were carriers.
checks.explanation: The parents are described as healthy elsewhere in the paper.

checks.claim: The MEGF10 C699S variant was not present in ClinVar.
checks.evidence_quote: This variant is absent in genomic databases (such as ClinVar and gnomAD)

checks.claim: The MEGF10 C699S variant was not present in gnomAD.
checks.evidence_quote: This variant is absent in genomic databases (such as ClinVar and gnomAD)

checks.claim: The MEGF10 C699S variant affects a conserved cysteine in an EGF-like domain.
checks.evidence_quote: the novel homozygous variant p.Cys699S affecting a very conserved cysteine residue in a crucial EGF-like functional domain

checks.claim: Croci et al. (2022) classified the MEGF10 C699S variant as likely pathogenic by ACMG criteria.
checks.evidence_quote: This amino acid change is further classified as likely pathogenic according to the ACMG criteria (PM2, PP3).
